title: SafeCompass: Dynamic Chain-of-Thought Steering via Inference-Time Safety Signals
claim: Our method breaks the robustness versus over-refusal trade-off, cutting attack success sharply while leaving benign behavior and safety awareness intact.
layout: 2 panels, left scatter with colorbar, right dual-axis bars with overlaid lines
description: The left panel is a scatter plot. Over-Refusal Rate runs along the x-axis and attack success rate (ASR) along the y-axis, and lower is better on both. Each baseline is a labeled dot: No-Defense, PSR, SP-ZS, SR, JA, RPO and SD. Dot color shows the Alpaca score on a viridis colorbar. A dashed diagonal runs through the plot. Our method sits alone at the bottom-left corner next to a small compass icon, which marks it as best. The right panel is a dual-axis bar chart with two groups, Jailbreak and Or-Bench. Hatched bars show ASR or over-refusal rate without SafeCompass (SC). Solid bars show the same rates with SC. A red line shows ASR dropping from 52% to 2%. Dashed black lines with markers show the safety score rising from -0.28 to 0.11 on Jailbreak. On Or-Bench the safety score stays near 0.15 to 0.17. The ASR and over-refusal rate fall from 1% to 1%, so they are unchanged. The eye goes first to the isolated bottom-left point and then to the tall hatched yellow bar.
caption: Left: Trade-off between average attack success rate (ASR) (across 9 jailbreak methods) and Over-Refusal Rate on Or-Bench. SafeCompass achieves the best performance (bottomleft). Right: SafeCompass effectively enhances safety scores and reduces ASR under jailbreak attacks, while preserving awareness on benign queries to prevent exaggerated refusals.
abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by explicitly generating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but this reasoning process can be manipulated by adversarial prompts. Inference-time CoT interventions offer a simple and lightweight approach to improving safety, yet existing methods typically apply static heuristics that ignore the dynamic nature of reasoning, leading to an inherent trade-off between robustness and over-refusal. This paper introduces *SafeCompass*, a plug-and-play framework for dynamically steering chain-of-thought reasoning using inference-time safety signals extracted from internal states. At different reasoning positions, *SafeCompass* derives a latent safety direction through contrastive analysis of internal representations and uses this direction to quantify the model’s current safety state. These signals enable selective intervention, allowing the model’s reasoning trajectory to be modified only when and where it becomes unsafe. Extensive experiments demonstrate that *SafeCompass* significantly improves robustness, reducing the average attack success rate up to $10\times$ compared to the best baseline, while preserving general reasoning performance and minimizing over-refusal rates.
